messages.body_plain:
> Also, what does it mean if the boxplot for a chip's exon-level NUSE
> suggests that this chip maybe an outlier (i.e. the median is higher
> than those of other chips), while its RLE boxplot doesn't suggest that
> (its RLE boxplot align with others)? Should I treat this chip as an
> outlier at all?

The NUSE is generally more sensitive than the RLE, so the NUSE will
often show a problem that the RLE misses.

> Another question I have been puzzled was:
> I noticed that exon-level NUSE boxplots typically show higher
> heterogeneity across chips, while gene-level NUSE boxplots don't. And
> RLE boxplots don't show much heterogeneity either at the exon-level or
> gene-level. Could someone give me an idea about why this is the case,
> and whether I should define an outlier based on the gene-level or exon-
> level NUSE/RLE?

The exon level NUSE will often be larger than the gene-level, and that's
because the NUSE is basically a measure per-gene of how much more
variable the sample is compared with the other samples. With only 4
probes (compared to all probes in a gene), its usually more variability
generally, so the boxplots are bigger. So they aren't really comparable.

Generally I find the gene-level NUSE the one that most frequently finds
the problems. But if there's any real obvious outlier in any of the
plots, then its a possible problem regardless of the other plots.
However, there is always variation and always one sample that will be
the worst, by definition, so make sure it does truly seem like an outlier.

Best,
Elizabeth

> > Also, what does it mean if the boxplot for a chip's exon-level NUSE
> > suggests that this chip maybe an outlier (i.e. the median is higher
> > than those of other chips), while its RLE boxplot doesn't suggest that
> > (its RLE boxplot align with others)? Should I treat this chip as an
> > outlier at all?
>
> The NUSE is generally more sensitive than the RLE, so the NUSE will
> often show a problem that the RLE misses.
>
> > Another question I have been puzzled was:
> > I noticed that exon-level NUSE boxplots typically show higher
> > heterogeneity across chips, while gene-level NUSE boxplots don't. And
> > RLE boxplots don't show much heterogeneity either at the exon-level or
> > gene-level. Could someone give me an idea about why this is the case,
> > and whether I should define an outlier based on the gene-level or exon-
> > level NUSE/RLE?
>
> The exon level NUSE will often be larger than the gene-level, and that's
> because the NUSE is basically a measure per-gene of how much more
> variable the sample is compared with the other samples. With only 4
> probes (compared to all probes in a gene), its usually more variability
> generally, so the boxplots are bigger. So they aren't really comparable.
>
> Generally I find the gene-level NUSE the one that most frequently finds
> the problems. But if there's any real obvious outlier in any of the
> plots, then its a possible problem regardless of the other plots.
> However, there is always variation and always one sample that will be
> the worst, by definition, so make sure it does truly seem like an outlier.

messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] more than two groups analysis using FIRMA
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chunjiang.

Thanks for reminding me to try and answer this question.

The general idea with differential splicing is that you are looking
for extreme FIRMA scores (large positive, large negative) as these
correspond to data that consistently (i.e. a whole probeset) stick out
from the expectation (specifically, the probe level linear model).
Most of this was studied in the context of a reasonably sized tissue
panel dataset, which gives a broad range of expression and a good
chance to tackle probe-specific effects.

When you are studying 2 or 3 or more groups with replicates, there is
less of a precedent for determining differential splicing.  But, it
seems logical to find FIRMA scores that are different b/w your 2+
groups, and that was my previous suggestion (using limma, say).  This
has been successful for us in the past.  I haven't found out the
reasons why SA thinks this is unconvincing.

There are all kinds of filtering that one might want to do as well:
for example, analysis of probes/probesets that overlap SNPs, low
expression etc.  I can't really give you a guide on what is most
reasonable.  Maybe others can comment.

Cheers,
Mark

As I mentioned before, I'd be careful with fitting models on
unnormalized data, but I'll assume you know what you are doing.

based?  Are your files on a local disk, or over a network mount?

Cheers,
Mark

First of all, I discovered a bug causing aroma.affymetrix to quietly
accept ASCII CDF files; the default is actually to thrown an
exception.  This bug will be fixed in the next release; I've also made
a patch available.

Note that it is extremely expensive to query ASCII CDF files.  It is
orders of magnitude faster to process binary files.  This is the most
likely cause of your slow processing speed.  You can use convertCdf()
of the affxparser package to convert an ASCII CDF files into a
binary/XDA CDF file.  I suggest that you use the same name for binary
CDF and stow away the ASCII CDF somewhere else.

...and no, the binary CDF is not created by default.  The reason why
it is faster when you run it the second time, is that the data is
already processed and hence not reprocessed.  The results are already
available (on file).

Note also that the (ASCII) CDF provided by Affymetrix that you use,
contains lots of units, which further adds to the processing time.  It
is also based on older annotation data.  See the chip type page
'HuEx-1_0-st-v2'

  http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/huex-1-0-st-v2

for alternative CDFs.  This has been discussed before on the mailing
list; check the archives.

})

If you see a non-zero number next to chr5, then that is the problem
and you'll have to remove those when you create the custom BPMAP.
Otherwise, post the output of that command and we'll have to
investigate further.

Mark

The reason we require startpos > 0 is that many of the BPMAP files
we've looked at have control antigenomic probes in them and these all
have startpos=0, so this was an easy way to filter them out.  I think
you are right though that startpos could start at 0, so your
workaround of setting it to 1 should be fine.

Of course, the bpmapCluster2Cdf() script is not meant to be a cure-all
for everyone's needs.  The source code is of course available to you
should you wish to do something different.

Cheers,
Mark

On 6-Dec-09, at 6:46 PM, Renyi Liu wrote:

> Hi, Mark,
>
> Thanks again for helping me with my previous question on CDF file. I
> have read your article on "Promoter 1.0R Tiling array analysis" and
> would like to apply MAT normalization to my dataset. Again, my dataset
> is from Arabidopsis and I need to create my own CDF file. For MAT
> analysis, we need to put copy number of probes into the bpmap file
> (and the CDF file). If you got a chance, I'd appreciate your help on a
> couple of more questions:

You may be able to use the BPMAP file for Arabidopsis from the MAT
website:

http://liulab.dfci.harvard.edu/MAT/Download.htm

... that would already have copy number in there.

> (1) should I filter out probes with copy number >10? (their xMAN paper
> states that they remove probes with copy number >10)

Yes, that's what they do for the BPMAP files at the MAT website.

> (2) for probes that map to multiple locations, how many entries need
> to included? (i.e. should I just randomly choose one of the mapping
> locations and put in startpos?). If multiple locations are included,
> the total number of probes will be much larger than the original
> affymetrix bpmap file.

You would want to keep all of them I guess, except for the >10 hits
that you've filtered.  So, yes, you would end up with more probes than
what you started with, but I'd expect that it wouldn't be *much*
larger, since (at least for human) only a small percentages of probes
map to multiple locations.

> (3) for MeDIP-chip data, which normalization method is the best choice
> in your opinion?

We typically use MAT for normalization, but you might be interested is
this comparison:

http://www.biomedcentral.com/1471-2105/10/204

Hope that helps.

Cheers,

Hi Libing.

I'm afraid that aroma.affymetrix will not work on TXT files.  I
suggest you check out the following functions in the 'affxparser'
package:

?readCel (just so you know what is stored)

?createCel (to create the file)
?updateCel (to store intensities in the file)

Once you figure out the inputs for those functions It should be pretty
straightforward to take your simulated data and push it into a CEL file.

Hope that helps.

Cheers,
Mark

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Distribute Aroma Objects As Rdata
messages.body_plain:
Hi.

No, saving "aroma" objects to .Rdata files using save()/save.image()
will not work the way you want.  Those objects are basically just
pointers to files on *your* file system - they do not contain any
data.  If you save such an object and reload it on another file
system, you will end up with an error reporting that the file is
missing.

Actually, I discourage saving "aroma" objects at all, but instead
always rerun the script from scratch; already processed steps will be
quickly done anyway.  If using save "aroma" object, there is a great
risk of unwanted errors.  Also, such saved objects may become obsolete
when new versions of aroma.affymetrix are released.  So, don't use
save() or save.image() for long-term purposes, but only locally on the
machine and for things such as restarting R or your machine, if at
all. FYI, I hardly ever use save()/save.image().

Back to the problem you're trying to solve.  It is on the to do list
to document how to migrate an already processed project/analysis.  It
is actually not that hard, you just need to identify the directories
where the raw/input data is sitting and the directories containing the
intermediate/final results.  [If anyone out there has the time to
contribute with an "how to" for this, it would be much appreciated.
Remember, this is an open-source project.]

Here is a stub on how to do a minimal data transfer (look for
generated subdirectories of probeData/, plmData/ and similar for
additional files to copy):

<stub>
How to: Migrate and reproduce an analysis elsewhere

Q: I've just finished a project.  How can my collaborators reproduce
the results on their machines?

A: In order to replicate an analysis, (1) the annotation data files,
(2) the raw data files, and (3) the R script need to be available.  By
transferring (1)-(3) to a new file system and rerunning the script
will reproduce the results exactly, given the same setup of packages
and version of R.  This should also be true if this is done between
different operating systems.  Here is what you need to do in order to
transfer the analysis to you collaborators:

   1. Identify and copy/zip the content of the raw data set
directory/directories, e.g. rawData/HapMap270,CEU/Mapping250K_Nsp/ and
rawData/HapMap270,CEU/Mapping250K_Sty/.
   2. Identify and copy/zip the content of the annotation chip type
directory/directories, e.g. annotationData/chipTypes/Mapping250K_Nsp/
and annotationData/chipTypes/Mapping250K_Sty/.  If there are auxillary
annotation files, you may want to copy only the ones used in the
analysis.
   3. Identify and copy/zip all R scripts.

Note that all of the above data is available from the current working
directory (either directly or via file/directory links).  Furthermore,
the R scripts should not have to be modified, but should work "as is"
regardless of location and operating system.  This is because the
aroma.* framework is designed to work without explicit file paths (if
you find that you have to specify a path, you are probably doing
something wrong).

It is good practice to always do the above and validate the
reproducible of any analysis completed, before passing it on to
collaborators or submitting to a journal.  When doing this one often
find minor discrepances such as not using the annotation files that
one believe one uses and so on.  It is also a good way to archive the
analysis done.
</stub>

Hope this helps

/Henrik

it is possible to migrate data from one file system to another -
aroma.affymetrix was actually designed for this purpose.  It is

document how to "Migrating all or parts of a project to another file
system", but the time is just not there yet.  However, the above
thread will give you enough details to figure it out yourself.

Finally, the first time you process a new chip type, you will
experience a "delay".  This is because several internal annotation
data files are constructed for that chip type.  As soon as they are
created, that will not be the case.  One such file is the
*,monocell.cdf file.  You'll find it under
annotationData/chipTypes/<your chip type>/.  You can copy this file to
your other file system to avoid having to recreate it there as well.

Hope this helps

Henrik

limFit to find the splicing events.

and B values from the topTable were very different.  I wonder what is
the right choice to fit my objective. Thanks

On Dec 4, 2:42 pm, Mark Robinson <mrobin...@wehi.EDU.AU> wrote:
> Hi Chunjiang.
>
> Thanks for reminding me to try and answer this question.
>
> The general idea with differential splicing is that you are looking
> for extreme FIRMA scores (large positive, large negative) as these
> correspond to data that consistently (i.e. a whole probeset) stick out
> from the expectation (specifically, the probe level linear model).
> Most of this was studied in the context of a reasonably sized tissue
> panel dataset, which gives a broad range of expression and a good
> chance to tackle probe-specific effects.
>
> When you are studying 2 or 3 or more groups with replicates, there is
> less of a precedent for determining differential splicing.  But, it
> seems logical to find FIRMA scores that are different b/w your 2+
> groups, and that was my previous suggestion (using limma, say).  This
> has been successful for us in the past.  I haven't found out the
> reasons why SA thinks this is unconvincing.
>
> There are all kinds of filtering that one might want to do as well:
> for example, analysis of probes/probesets that overlap SNPs, low
> expression etc.  I can't really give you a guide on what is most
> reasonable.  Maybe others can comment.
